2. Social Class

Social class system is the most common form of stratification in modern world

Boundaries are fluid, allows social mobility

Both an ascribed and an achieved status

Children are ascribed with the status of their parents, but they can achieve their own social class when they grow up

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology05 / 42
Slide 05

Definition

A social class is a category of people with approximately the same amount of wealth, status, and power in a society (a.k.a. socioeconomic status (SES))

Different models exist:

E.g., A Five-class model:

Upper class

Upper-middle class

Lower-middle class

Working class

Lower class

E.g., A Two-class model:

bourgeoisie (those who control the means of production; purchase labors)

vs.

proletariats (those who do not control the means of production but have to sell their labor for a living; they are exploited by the bourgeoisie)

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology07 / 42
Education

A resource-generating resource

Education brings economic benefits - better occupation, higher income, and low economic hardship

Education develops human capital: analytic and problem-solving skills, critical/complex thinking ability, learning ability, self-esteem, sense of mastery (as opposed to sense of powerlessness, fatalism, and helplessness)

Education develops social capital: access to social networks including people with power and resources

Education develops cultural (symbolic) capital: socially valued habits, preferences, cultural knowledge and behaviors (i.e., highbrow vs. lowbrow)

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology19 / 42
Income & Wealth

Income: a flow of money from any resources, such as, business, wages, rent, interest, royalties, alimony, allowance, or even gambling.

income captures the flow of economic resources (such as wages) into the household

Wealth: total value of property minus all debts; it is the net worth of a person;

wealth captures the accumulated economic resources that are reflected in savings, home equity, and other financial assets.

Measuring “Opportunity”: Social Mobility

Social mobility – is a measure of the change in an individual’s socioeconomic status either in the person’s own lifetime or across generations;

Upward Mobility – a change in a person's social status resulting in that person receiving a higher position

Downward Mobility- a change resulting in a lower position

Inter-generational Mobility - a change that occurs from one generation to the next

Intra-generational Mobility – mobility within a single generation’s lifetime

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology37 / 42
Slide 37

Social Mobility

Absolute Mobility –upward/downward change of income/wealth over time;

Relative Mobility – upward/downward change of one’s rank in the overall income/wealth distribution.
